slides.say: Eight children all have different heights. A photographer chooses seven of them and places them in a row from shortest to tallest. How many different rows can be formed?
at: Eight children all have different heights

slides.say: So we choose seven of eight, and their order is forced, from shortest to tallest. This one is medium plus, maybe even hard.
We'll solve it in two different ways. Let's start by plugging in numbers, with trial and error. We give the heights the numbers one to eight. One is the shortest, and eight is the tallest.
at: We give the heights the numbers

slides.say: Now we build rows of seven, always from shortest to tallest. The first row is one to seven.
at: The first row is one to seven

slides.say: To stay organized, we change only the right end. We swap the seven for an eight.
at: We swap the seven for an eight

slides.say: Next, we leave out the six instead. One to five, then seven and eight.
And we keep moving the missing child one place to the left, until we leave out the one.
No more options. That's eight rows.
Let's check against the choices. Seven is too few, because we already found eight different rows.
Five thousand forty is seven factorial. That would let the seven stand in any order, but here the order is forced. Far too many, and fifty-six is too many as well, because we found every row.
at: Five thousand forty is seven factorial

slides.say: [pause] Now the insight. Imagine you are the photographer. Instead of choosing seven children, you choose the one child who stays out.
You say to one child, you stay. Everyone else, come here. And they line up from shortest to tallest, in only one way.
Any of the eight children can be the one who stays out. So that's eight options.
This is the complementary event. It isn't magic. It's a technique worth knowing, and it helps in many questions.
Choice number three is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number three is our answer
